passage: I'm Sahil. When Rehana admitted she had pushed a change without testing and broken the build, I could see her bracing. So I told her about the worst project of my early career: a billing module I insisted on rewriting alone, then hid my delays for weeks, and shipped late with bugs that cost a client an evening of manual work. I kept it to three minutes, no dramatic ending, because this wasn't my moment. What I learned, I said, was that telling the team early would have saved everyone time. Then I turned it back to her: 'What would you want the team to know about yesterday?' Rehana let out a breath and began to explain. Later she said it was easier to talk once she knew I had stumbled too.

qa.q: How long did Sahil's story take?
qa.a: Sahil kept it to three minutes.

qa.q: What did Sahil want to make sure of while telling the story?
qa.a: Sahil was concerned that Rehana was bracing herself, so Sahil kept the story short and turned it back to her, making sure the talk stayed about her.

qa.q: What could Sahil do if Rehana still stayed quiet about the mistake?
qa.a: Sahil could offer to go through the change together on a shared screen, since working side by side takes away some of the pressure of explaining.

qa.q: How did the story feel to Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana felt relieved and safer: she let out a breath, and later said it was easier to talk knowing Sahil had stumbled too. 🙂

grounding: Shows a mentor telling a short honest story of a past bad project and its lesson so the mentee can admit a mistake, without making the story about themselves.

passage:
Yash: Bhai, how do I apply for a master's abroad? Deadlines are close.
Kishore: Easy. Do your exam first, then send applications at the end of the month. Universities don't mind late ones.
Yash: Really? Nothing needed before that?
Kishore: Trust me, everyone does it that way 👍
[three weeks later]
Yash: Kishore, two universities say their deadline was last week 😟
Yash: I waited like you said
Kishore: Oh no. I've never actually applied abroad. I assumed it works like our college admissions. I should have said I don't know.
Yash: Now I've probably lost a year
Kishore: Let's find someone who has done it. The universities' international offices can give exact dates too. I'm sorry.
Yash: ok. Thanks for saying it.

qa.q: When did Yash learn that two universities had passed their deadlines?
qa.a: Yash learned it three weeks later.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after Yash's message about the deadlines?
qa.a: Kishore felt regretful and ashamed, admitting to never having applied abroad and to having assumed it worked like college admissions.

qa.q: What could Kishore have done when Yash first asked?
qa.a: Kishore could have said honestly that Kishore did not know the process and pointed Yash to an international office or someone who had applied.

qa.q: How might Yash be feeling about the lost year?
qa.a: Yash is probably worried and disappointed, though thanking Kishore for the honesty suggests some trust remains.

grounding: Shows a mentor giving confident advice on applying abroad without knowing the process, so the mentee waits and misses deadlines.

subtype: Approach: connecting the mentee to other people [Action]
passage: I'm Zoya, and I share a desk with Dhruv, so I hear his mentoring calls. On Thursday Maria asked about switching into data journalism, and Dhruv said, 'That's outside what I know, I'd only be guessing.' I noticed he didn't leave it there. He picked up his phone, messaged a friend who works at a news desk, and wrote, 'My mentee Maria is thinking about your line of work. Could you give her twenty minutes?' Then he told Maria the friend's name and said he'd check in after the chat. Maria looked surprised, maybe a little nervous, and copied the name into her notes. A week later Maria mentioned that the friend had also introduced her to a reporter who ran a small open data project.

qa.q: What did Dhruv say when Maria asked about data journalism?
qa.a: Dhruv said, 'That's outside what I know, I'd only be guessing.'

qa.q: What might Maria have been feeling when Dhruv passed on the friend's name?
qa.a: Maria seemed surprised and maybe a little nervous, as Zoya notes, though Maria may also have felt grateful.

qa.q: What could Dhruv add to help Maria use the twenty minutes well?
qa.a: Dhruv could ask Maria to prepare two questions beforehand, so the short chat with the friend is spent on what matters most to her.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's friend at the news desk see the request?
qa.a: The friend probably sees a colleague who trusts them and may be glad to help, since twenty minutes is a modest ask.

grounding: Shows a mentor who, faced with a question outside their area, introduces the mentee to a friend in that field.

subtype: Approach: adapting to the mentee's style and background [Revision]
passage: I'm Joseph, and I mentored Rajni for a year. Rajni was the first in the family to finish college, and in our early meetings I'd ask, 'Any questions?' and get, 'No, sir, all clear.' Then Rajni's work would come back with the same doubts, unasked. Around the fourth session I noticed the pattern and realised my plan, with questions put on the spot, suited me and not Rajni. So I changed. I began sending a short note two days before each meeting with the topics, and Rajni wrote questions back on paper. In the room I left a few quiet minutes with nothing to say. The first question that came out of that silence was a real one, about how to ask for feedback. Others kept coming.

qa.q: Around which session did Joseph notice the pattern?
qa.a: Joseph noticed it around the fourth session.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when the same doubts came back unasked?
qa.a: Joseph was puzzled and concerned that the mentoring was not reaching Rajni, which led Joseph to rethink the plan.

qa.q: What other change could Joseph try for Rajni?
qa.a: Joseph could ask how Rajni likes to learn and open a message channel for questions between meetings, since some people find asking in writing easier.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt in the quiet minutes?
qa.a: Rajni probably felt less pressed, having time to think, since the first real question came out of that silence.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing that a shy first-generation graduate does not ask questions, and switching to written notes before meetings and quiet time.

subtype: Approach: guarding own time and limits [Thinking]
passage: Sunday night. A third person asked me to mentor them this week, and I said no. It was awkward. Last spring I had four mentees plus the release crunch, and I cancelled on two of them; one went quiet and I'm not sure I ever fixed that. So the rule now: two at a time, Tuesday and Thursday evenings, forty-five minutes, and I say so upfront. Hemant is one of my two, and I'd rather give Hemant a reliable slot than a maybe. Wrote to the third person offering to recommend a colleague and a date when I might have space. Felt guilty for an hour, then fine. Sessions kept beat sessions promised. — Tejas

qa.q: How many mentees does Tejas take at a time?
qa.a: Tejas takes two mentees at a time.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel after saying no to the third request?
qa.a: Tejas felt guilty for an hour and then fine, having protected the sessions already promised.

qa.q: What other approach could Tejas use for people who ask but cannot fit in?
qa.a: Tejas could run a group session once a month for those people, which shares some help without a weekly promise.

qa.q: How might Hemant see the arrangement?
qa.a: Hemant probably feels secure that sessions will happen, having a reliable slot instead of a maybe.

grounding: Shows a mentor limiting the number of mentees, stating availability clearly and keeping the commitment reliable.

subtype: Approach: reviewing progress and ending gracefully [Revision]
passage: Saturday. Six months since I started meeting Sangeeta, so today's session was a review. We went through the list from January. Done: portfolio site, two mock interviews, and a first proper offer letter. Not done: the open-source contribution. Sangeeta said she still wants it, so it stays, but on her own with a check-in from me. Then I raised the thing I'd been putting off: maybe we don't need regular sessions anymore. I worried it would sound like I was pulling away. Sangeeta grinned and said she'd been thinking the same and would rather message me when stuck. So we're moving to one catch-up every two months, plus messages anytime. Strange, but it feels like a finish line, not a door closing. — Naveen

qa.q: Which goal was not finished?
qa.a: The open-source contribution was not finished.

qa.q: What did Naveen worry about when raising the change?
qa.a: Naveen worried that it would sound like Naveen was pulling away.

qa.q: What other step could Naveen offer Sangeeta after regular sessions end?
qa.a: Naveen could offer a one-off session before any big decision, such as a job choice, since it keeps support available without a fixed rota.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see the move to occasional check-ins?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably sees it as a good step, since she had been thinking the same and would rather message when stuck.

grounding: Shows a mentor and mentee reviewing goals achieved after six months and agreeing to occasional check-ins, treating the end of regular sessions as success.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: At a Saturday workshop in a community centre in Indore, Tanvir, a software tester, was handed a sheet titled 'What keeps pulling you?' Vinita, the facilitator, asked everyone to list problems they kept reading about or raising without being asked. Tanvir wrote quickly: village school dropouts, water quality in the old city, and, after a pause, lonely elderly neighbours. Vinita's second question was, 'Which of these fit what you can actually do?' Tanvir crossed out the third, since it needed skills Tanvir didn't have, and circled the first. 'I can build simple tools, and I keep thinking about the school in my grandfather's village.' Vinita asked one more thing: 'Whose voices haven't you heard yet?' Tanvir wrote it as the first line under the circle: talk to the teachers.

qa.q: What was the title of the sheet Tanvir was handed?
qa.a: The sheet was titled 'What keeps pulling you?'

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel about the third problem, and why was it crossed out?
qa.a: Tanvir cared about it, but felt unequipped, since it needed skills Tanvir didn't have.

qa.q: What other approach could Tanvir use to test the first choice?
qa.a: Tanvir could volunteer for a month with a local group working on school dropouts, since real contact shows whether the interest lasts.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Tanvir's choice?
qa.a: Vinita probably sees a sensible one, joining a real concern to real skills, with a first step of listening to teachers.

grounding: Shows a person asking which problems keep drawing their attention and which fit their skills before choosing a purpose project.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: starting with a small pilot [Action]
passage: Saturday, 9 pm. First class done. Twenty students from classes eight to ten in the school near my aunt's village crammed into one room with six borrowed laptops. Neelam, the science teacher who let me use the room, sat at the back. I'd planned an hour on variables; it took forty minutes because half the group couldn't type yet, so we switched to drawing flowcharts on paper and typing in pairs. Learned already: pairs work, short tasks work, my slides don't. The power went out twice, and the kids clapped in the dark when it came back. I'm not planning anything big yet. Four more Saturdays, then I'll write down what worked and only then decide what next. Tired feet, full head. — Farida

qa.q: How many laptops were there?
qa.a: There were six borrowed laptops.

qa.q: How does Farida feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Farida feels tired but energised, with tired feet and a full head from what was learned.

qa.q: What other approach could Farida use before the next class?
qa.a: Farida could ask Neelam and a few students what they want to learn, since it shows what is worth teaching before more slides are made.

qa.q: How might Neelam see the class?
qa.a: Neelam probably sees a useful start, since twenty students turned up and stayed engaged even when the power went out.

grounding: Shows a software worker starting with free Saturday coding classes for twenty village school students and learning what works before planning anything larger.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: grand vision with no first step [Pitfall]
passage: For eight months Kiran told anyone who'd listen about the plan to transform education across the state. There was a forty-slide deck, three logo options, and a name argued over with Manoj, a friend, on long tea breaks. Kiran also had a full-time job and only Sunday mornings free. Whenever Manoj asked, 'What can we do this month?' Kiran said the idea was too big for small steps. Teaching one class felt silly next to a whole state. One Sunday a heavy monsoon kept the two indoors, and Manoj asked to see the calendar: not one meeting with a school, not one test of an idea. The deck was polished, and nothing else existed. Kiran closed the laptop and said nothing for a while.

qa.q: How many logo options did Kiran have?
qa.a: Kiran had three logo options.

qa.q: Why did Kiran resist small steps?
qa.a: Kiran felt the dream was so large that teaching one class seemed silly next to a whole state, so any first step felt too small.

qa.q: What other approach could Kiran use to get started?
qa.a: Kiran could pick one school and run a small pilot on a Sunday morning, since a real class would teach more than another version of the deck.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the deck and the months of talk?
qa.a: Manoj probably sees a lot of effort with nothing tested and feels frustrated, and asking to see the calendar shows worry for Kiran.

grounding: Shows a person with a huge dream to change education, months of presentations and logos, and no first action, because the size makes small steps seem pointless.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: listening to the community before designing [Action]
passage:
Mridul: Back from the village. So glad I went before ordering books.
Bidisha: Tell me. What did they say?
Mridul: Talked to eight parents and three teachers, on the school steps and one evening at the tea stall.
Mridul: Everyone said the same thing: kids can't study after dark. Power cuts, and one bulb at home.
Bidisha: Not more books? 😮
Mridul: Books came third. First lighting, second a quiet room with a table.
Bidisha: So the library becomes a study room with a lamp?
Mridul: Yes 🙂 The panchayat hall is empty in the evenings, and one teacher offered to hold the key.
Bidisha: Then what are you buying first?
Mridul: Two solar lamps and six mats. Books later, when the kids tell me what they want.

qa.q: How many parents and teachers did Mridul talk to?
qa.a: Mridul talked to eight parents and three teachers.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel about going to the village first?
qa.a: Mridul felt glad and relieved to have listened before ordering books, since it changed the whole plan.

qa.q: What could Mridul do next to check the plan works?
qa.a: Mridul could open the room for a week and ask families what changes they notice, since real use shows what to adjust.

qa.q: How might the teacher who offered to hold the key see the plan?
qa.a: The teacher probably feels supportive and hopeful, since offering the key shows trust in the idea.

grounding: Shows a person talking with parents and teachers in a village and learning that evening light and study space matter more than new books.
